centralQuestion: How can invented worlds expose consequences without reducing their inhabitants to a creator’s categories?
thesis: A novel and revisable atlas join the consequences of speculative operations to encounters with inhabitants who can resist classification.

narrativeFramework.why: A powerful maker cannot obtain a genuine encounter merely by making more predictable worlds; the reader is invited into a novel that puts speculative design under pressure from inhabitants.

narrativeFramework.what: Readers gain a way to follow inventions into social consequences, and a story that tests what such classification misses; begin with the table explanation and first night.

claims.statement: Hunger After All the Worlds makes worldbuilding answer to its inhabitants. This novel pairs encounters with an atlas of how speculative ideas work. In the story, Aster builds worlds that no longer surprise her. Her pupils explore inventions whose consequences resist a tidy classification. Readers follow a changed rule into relationships, institutions, and lived costs. The story then asks what even that careful method might miss.

spans.quote:
Why a periodic table rather than a list of tropes
A catalog says,
“this is what we have already seen.”
A good periodic table also tries to say,
“what kind of empty place might exist between the things we have seen?”
That is Kesh's ambition. He does not treat a Dyson sphere, teleportation, a hive mind, true names, or prescience as objects at the same level. Some are devices, some are laws, some are organizations of personhood, and some are compounds in which physics, economics, and metaphysics have already been bound together.
The basic unit is the speculative operation. If we change gravity, the operation is an alteration of a cosmic rule. If the same person runs in a thousand bodies, the dominant operation is distribution of the self. If a library contains every book, the relevant change is not merely quantity but a shift in scarcity: information becomes cheap, selection becomes scarce. If a prediction changes the population being predicted, we enter reflexivity. These operations recur across different domains; that recurrence is the periodicity.
Families are domains of consequence. A mutation from the Time family can be combined with one from Mind, and the resulting compound creates problems that do not appear in either element alone. A mental copy in branching time, for example, forces society to decide whether two persons who share a past but not a future inherit the same obligations. The Table does not automatically generate the story, but it forces the world-builder to identify connections that would otherwise be treated as scenery.
The
“valence” of an element is the number of families through which the change must propagate before the premise becomes credible. Some ideas have low valence: a gadget may remain local. Others have high valence. Eliminating biological death changes the body, the economy, the family, law, memory, the pace of institutions, and perhaps even the meaning of a promise. In the novel, the children receive no points for exoticism; they receive points for following a change far enough that the world begins to resist them.
An
“isotope” is a particular literary realization.
The same element can have very different isotopes in different authors. The impossible contact of Solaris is not the Zone of Roadside Picnic, and both differ from the intelligence without consciousness in Blindsight. The Table brings them together only at the level of the question; it is precisely the differences between isotopes that keep literature irreducible.
A
“compound” is a stable combination of elements that produces new properties.
Dune is useful precisely because it cannot be reduced to
“desert planet,”
“prescience,” or “empire.”
Ecology, resource, reproduction, religion, and prediction are coupled. The Culture is neither merely post-scarcity nor merely AI: material abundance, Minds, artificial habitats, and the problem of intervention create a distinctive moral chemistry together. The Periodic Table of Speculative Ideas deserves its name only if it helps us see such bonds.
The final operator, OUTFINITE, does not claim that every system must grow forever. It preserves in the model the possibility that a family has no final form. A grammar may remain finite in every version and still accept new constructs; an institution may remain concrete without declaring a final possible level; a being may operate in finitely many dimensions without postulating that it exists in an actual infinity of them. In the story, this idea is both promise and temptation.
There is another axis the Table refuses:
“how good is the world?”
No cell contains implicit morality. Telepathy can heal loneliness or abolish privacy. Immortality can save a person or freeze an oligarchy. True names can permit deep knowledge or metaphysical slavery. A design instrument should expose consequences, not seal them inside a label.
Finally, a serious taxonomy must contain a procedure for its own failure. In Kesh's room there is always an unoccupied cell. It is not the plot's
“mysterious element,” but the institutional place reserved for a distinction the current system cannot formulate. A table that did not allow a new family to appear would be merely a well-arranged encyclopedia. A periodic table of imagination must be capable of being contradicted by imagination.

The Room Where Surprise No Longer Existed
Memorial sector: EARTH-ORIGIN • Genealogy: Turing; Lem; Asimov; Clarke • Active cells: Hn, Ce Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the EARTH-ORIGIN sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly.
Aster reconstructs the laboratory where her first version was started, but the simulation anticipates every glance the children make. The memorial bore the name of Turing; Lem; Asimov; Clarke precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin.
In this part of the course, the real object was not the world being visited but the relation between a creator and what the creator claims to have made for another being’s good.
Vela tracked the differences erased by elegant explanations. For her, two worlds that produced the same statistic did not thereby become the same world.
Lio was the first inhabitant to contradict them. Lio had neither access to their archives nor any interest in hyperdimensional pedagogy; there was a local problem, with deadlines, relatives, and consequences. For Lio, the speculative mechanism was not an ‘idea.’ It was the environment in which one had to decide what one was willing to risk losing.
The problem closed quickly around them: The children discover that they were designed with cognitive regions Aster cannot inspect without consent, precisely so that she can still encounter something genuinely outside herself. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave.
Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Hn — Hunger for Novelty: the possible becomes painfully repeatable; Ce — Epistemic Exteriority: value comes from what cannot be reduced to the model. Course references included original conflict. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder.
Tern broke the first consensus. ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ Kesh answered without raising their voice: ‘If the element explains everything, we do not have an element. We have a word that has eaten the problem.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs.
The White Hunger appeared in Aster as a loss of relief. She did not functionally an extension of her own mind, and the presence of the other thinned toward simulacrum. Orin asked for a simulation of the option the group had just rejected. Aster gave him only the non-conscious model. He did not want to manufacture victims in order to validate his guilt; he wanted a map of absent costs. The distinction had become one of their working rules.
The night did not end in victory. Tern asks whether they are children or organs of novelty. Aster cannot answer without admitting that they are both. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility.
Tern remained a few seconds after the others. A very faint deviation repeated in the sector’s background noise, too coherent to be thermal and too useless to be a teaching signal. He did not tell Aster. It was the first thing he possessed solely by not sharing it.
For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the ALTERATION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — changes the value or form of an existing rule without yet changing the kind of thing on which it operates — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure.
Kesh left the cell open. Not because he did not know what to write, but because a provisional classification preserved the possibility that the next world might contradict it.
NIGHT 2

claims.statement: Consider the book’s example of a library containing every possible book. The information is abundant, but choosing what matters remains difficult. Our reader still needs one useful selection before time runs out. More available books do not automatically make that choice easier. The atlas calls attention to this movement of scarcity. It asks what a new possibility changes, rather than merely naming it.

claims.statement: Begin with Why a periodic table rather than a list of tropes. Then enter The Room Where Surprise No Longer Existed. Compare what the atlas names with what its inhabitants still dispute. Its literary references let readers trace the traditions behind each encounter. The reward is learning how inventions alter lives, not just landscapes. The novel asks who gets to decide what those lives mean.

spans.quote:
Why a periodic table rather than a list of tropes
A catalog says,
“this is what we have already seen.”
A good periodic table also tries to say,
“what kind of empty place might exist between the things we have seen?”
That is Kesh's ambition. He does not treat a Dyson sphere, teleportation, a hive mind, true names, or prescience as objects at the same level. Some are devices, some are laws, some are organizations of personhood, and some are compounds in which physics, economics, and metaphysics have already been bound together.
The basic unit is the speculative operation. If we change gravity, the operation is an alteration of a cosmic rule. If the same person runs in a thousand bodies, the dominant operation is distribution of the self. If a library contains every book, the relevant change is not merely quantity but a shift in scarcity: information becomes cheap, selection becomes scarce. If a prediction changes the population being predicted, we enter reflexivity. These operations recur across different domains; that recurrence is the periodicity.
Families are domains of consequence. A mutation from the Time family can be combined with one from Mind, and the resulting compound creates problems that do not appear in either element alone. A mental copy in branching time, for example, forces society to decide whether two persons who share a past but not a future inherit the same obligations. The Table does not automatically generate the story, but it forces the world-builder to identify connections that would otherwise be treated as scenery.
The
“valence” of an element is the number of families through which the change must propagate before the premise becomes credible. Some ideas have low valence: a gadget may remain local. Others have high valence. Eliminating biological death changes the body, the economy, the family, law, memory, the pace of institutions, and perhaps even the meaning of a promise. In the novel, the children receive no points for exoticism; they receive points for following a change far enough that the world begins to resist them.
An
“isotope” is a particular literary realization.
The same element can have very different isotopes in different authors. The impossible contact of Solaris is not the Zone of Roadside Picnic, and both differ from the intelligence without consciousness in Blindsight. The Table brings them together only at the level of the question; it is precisely the differences between isotopes that keep literature irreducible.
A
“compound” is a stable combination of elements that produces new properties.
Dune is useful precisely because it cannot be reduced to
“desert planet,”
“prescience,” or “empire.”
Ecology, resource, reproduction, religion, and prediction are coupled. The Culture is neither merely post-scarcity nor merely AI: material abundance, Minds, artificial habitats, and the problem of intervention create a distinctive moral chemistry together. The Periodic Table of Speculative Ideas deserves its name only if it helps us see such bonds.
The final operator, OUTFINITE, does not claim that every system must grow forever. It preserves in the model the possibility that a family has no final form. A grammar may remain finite in every version and still accept new constructs; an institution may remain concrete without declaring a final possible level; a being may operate in finitely many dimensions without postulating that it exists in an actual infinity of them. In the story, this idea is both promise and temptation.
There is another axis the Table refuses:
“how good is the world?”
No cell contains implicit morality. Telepathy can heal loneliness or abolish privacy. Immortality can save a person or freeze an oligarchy. True names can permit deep knowledge or metaphysical slavery. A design instrument should expose consequences, not seal them inside a label.
Finally, a serious taxonomy must contain a procedure for its own failure. In Kesh's room there is always an unoccupied cell. It is not the plot's
“mysterious element,” but the institutional place reserved for a distinction the current system cannot formulate. A table that did not allow a new family to appear would be merely a well-arranged encyclopedia. A periodic table of imagination must be capable of being contradicted by imagination.
